# @sanity/workflow-cli

Command-line tool for deploying, inspecting, and administering Sanity workflow
definitions and instances.

The package is in early access and is publicly available on npm. Commands that
access Sanity use the resources in `sanity.workflow.ts` and authenticate with a
login session or an API token. `deploy --check` validates definitions and
checks the generated runtime offline, and `definitions validate` checks
definition JSON files without a config.

## Run

Use Node.js 20.12 or later. Install the CLI and its engine peer from the same
Workflows release in your project:

```sh
npm install --save-dev @sanity/workflow-cli @sanity/workflow-engine
npx @sanity/workflow-cli --help
```

After authentication and [configuration](#configuration), run commands through
the project-local package:

```sh
npx @sanity/workflow-cli deploy --dry-run
npx @sanity/workflow-cli list --include-completed
npx @sanity/workflow-cli show INSTANCE_ID
```

Replace `INSTANCE_ID` with the workflow instance ID returned by `list`.

The package is an [oclif](https://oclif.io) plugin: every command's canonical
id nests under the `workflows` topic
(`sanity-workflows workflows deploy`), so the `sanity` CLI runs the same
commands as `sanity workflows …` without colliding with its own root
commands (the sanity CLI already has a `deploy`). The short forms used
throughout this README (`deploy`, `definitions list`, …) are the standalone
binary's stable surface — its production and development entrypoints
(`bin/run.js` and `bin/dev.js`) rewrite them onto the topic before oclif
resolves the command. Those short forms are **not** registered as oclif aliases,
so a host mount does not pollute the host root.

Authenticate with `npx sanity@latest login`; the CLI reads that session token.
For CI, set `SANITY_AUTH_TOKEN` instead. Create a `sanity.workflow.ts` in your
project, as described in [Configuration](#configuration).

The token must span **every resource the workflow references**, not just the
workflow resource. Runtime commands build one client from the deployment
descriptor; when a workflow's subject or `doc.ref` fields point into other
datasets (or a canvas / media library), the engine reaches them through
sibling clients derived from that same token. A `sanity login` session or an
org-capable token covers this out of the box; a token scoped to a single
project will fail on cross-resource reads.

## Configuration

The CLI is configured by a `sanity.workflow.ts` (or `.js`/`.mjs`). It looks in
the directory you run from, then in each parent directory, and uses the first
one it finds. Pass `--path` to name a config file, or a directory to start the
search from. Wherever you run the command, `blueprints generate` writes the
generated Blueprint files next to the config file, and `deploy` checks them
there.

The file exports a config built with `defineWorkflowConfig`, declaring your
**deployments** (typically one per environment):

```ts
import type {WorkflowDeploymentInput} from '@sanity/workflow-engine'
import {defineWorkflowConfig} from '@sanity/workflow-engine/define'

import {articleReview, urlDraft} from './src/workflows.ts'

// Export each deployment under its own `name`, then list the exports in the
// config. `blueprints generate` requires these named exports, and so does
// `deploy` once a generated runtime sits next to this file; nothing else does.
export const production = {
  expectedMinReaderModel: 4,
  name: 'production', // the deployment's unique identity (lowercase letters, digits, dashes)
  partition: 'prod', // the environment partition the engine's docs are scoped to
  workflowResource: {type: 'dataset', id: 'acme.workflows'}, // where those docs live
  resourceAliases: [
    // binds each `@<handle>:` a definition references to a physical resource
    // in a DIFFERENT dataset from `workflowResource` (same-resource content
    // needs no alias — see below)
    {name: 'content', resource: {type: 'dataset', id: 'acme.content'}},
    {name: 'assets', resource: {type: 'dataset', id: 'acme.assets'}},
  ],
  definitions: [articleReview, urlDraft], // the batch this deployment ships
} satisfies WorkflowDeploymentInput

export default defineWorkflowConfig({deployments: [production]})
```

`name` is the deployment's identity: unique across the config and constrained
to the same grammar as `partition`. Partitions group deployments by environment and may
repeat, as long as no two deployments share both a `workflowResource` and a
`partition`. The config rejects that collision and names both deployments.

For `deploy`, `start`, `definitions diff`, and `definitions delete`, select a
deployment with `--deployment <name>`. With one deployment configured, you can
omit the selector. `--partition <partition>` selects one deployment when the partition is unique;
on `deploy`, it targets every deployment carrying the partition. With several
deployments and no selector, these commands prompt for a deployment in an
interactive terminal. In a non-interactive shell, they fail asking for
`--deployment` or `--partition`; `deploy` also suggests `--all-partitions`.

The instance-targeted commands `abort`, `set-stage`, `reset-activity`,
`fire-action`, `diagnose`, `show`, and `tail` locate the instance by ID across
configured resources. Their optional `--deployment` and `--partition` flags
narrow the resources searched; the operation's partition comes from the loaded
instance.

`list`, `definitions list`, and `definitions show` read every configured resource
and partition by default. `--partition` filters to one partition, and
`--deployment` reads only that deployment's resource and partition.

The read commands `list`, `show`, `tail`, `diagnose`, `definitions list`, and
`definitions show` can also read one resource you name, with or without a
`sanity.workflow.ts`. Use the same flags as the Sanity CLI:
`--project-id <id>` and `--dataset <name>` (`-p` and `-d`) together for a
dataset, or `--media-library-id <id>` for a media library. The CLI then reads
only that resource and loads no config, so `--deployment` and `--path` can't be
combined with them. `--partition` still filters. Commands that write, such as
`start`, `abort`, and `deploy`, always act through a deployment in
`sanity.workflow.ts`.

```sh
sanity workflows definitions list --project-id abc123 --dataset production
sanity workflows show prod.wf-instance.x7k2 -p abc123 -d production
```

When an instance ID or definition name is found in more than one deployment,
for example two deployments on different resources that both use `default`,
an interactive terminal prompts you to pick one. Each choice shows the
deployment name with its dataset. With `--json` or in a non-interactive shell,
the command fails, lists each candidate as `name (dataset)`, and asks for
`--deployment`.

A deployment alone on its configured resource may omit `partition`; it resolves
to `default`, independent of its name. If several deployments share that
resource, give every one an explicit, distinct partition. The engine stores the
partition on every definition and instance the deployment writes, so a
deployment only reaches documents written under its own partition value.

`--all-partitions` deploys every deployment in the config in one run: a failure in one doesn't
stop the rest — the run continues, prints a summary of what failed, and exits
non-zero. The client's project + dataset are derived from the deployment's
`workflowResource`, and `deploy` expands each definition's `@<handle>:`
reference to the bound physical resource. An invalid config fails with a clean,
path-prefixed error before the command runs.

`resourceAliases` is only for content that lives in a _different_ resource from
`workflowResource`. A definition can reference a document in the **same**
resource by bare id, no alias needed — bare ids root at `workflowResource` at
runtime. `@<handle>:` references exist at deploy time only: `deploy` expands
each one to its bound physical GDR, and nothing alias-shaped survives into the
deployed definition or the runtime. Rule of thumb: **different resource →
bind an alias; same resource → use a bare id and omit `resourceAliases`
entirely.** So the simplest single-dataset setup is just a `workflowResource`
and `definitions`, with no `resourceAliases` at all.

Refs supplied at runtime (`start --field`, `fire-action` ref params) are gated
separately: they may target the `workflowResource` itself or any resource the
deployment binds in `resourceAliases`, and anything else is rejected at the
write with `RefResourceUndeclaredError`. To start a workflow on content in
another dataset or project, bind that resource even when no definition
references the alias. The CLI reaches each bound resource with the same token
and API host it uses for `workflowResource`, so that login must be a member of
every bound project. Instance commands use the bindings of the configured
deployment that owns the instance's partition on the resource it was found in.
When no configured deployment owns that partition, refs may target only the
workflow resource.

| Var                 | Purpose                                                                                              |
| ------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `SANITY_AUTH_TOKEN` | Explicit token for CI / scripted use — wins over the `sanity login` session (editor role for writes) |
| `SANITY_API_HOST`   | Optional API host override (defaults to the prod API)                                                |

Run through the `dev` / `cli` scripts and the CLI itself and your
`sanity.workflow.ts` load straight from TypeScript source: the scripts set
`NODE_OPTIONS='--conditions=development'` under `tsx`, and the config file is
transpiled on the fly by `jiti`. Definitions you author **inline** in the
config, or import by **relative path**, transpile the same way — no build step.

One caveat: a definition imported from a _separate workspace package_ (e.g.
`@sanity/workflow-examples`) resolves to that package's built `dist/`. `jiti`
applies its own module resolution and does **not** honour
`--conditions=development`, so it never picks up a package's `src/` export
condition — rebuild that package after editing it, or the config loads its
stale compiled output.

> [!NOTE]
> pnpm intercepts a handful of its own flag names (`--check`,
> `--filter`, `--recursive`, …) when they appear after a script name.
> To invoke `deploy --check`, run from inside the package or via
> `pnpm exec`:
>
> ```bash
> # from inside packages/workflow-cli
> pnpm dev deploy --check
>
> # or, from anywhere
> pnpm --filter @sanity/workflow-cli exec \
>   env NODE_OPTIONS='--conditions=development' \
>   tsx --env-file-if-exists=../../.env bin/dev.js deploy --check
> ```
>
> `--dry-run` and `--only` don't collide with pnpm flags and work
> through the normal `pnpm --filter … dev …` invocation.

## Command list

Invoke as `sanity workflows <command>` in the Sanity CLI, or `sanity-workflows <command>` through the standalone binary. Suggested next commands in the output use whichever form you ran.

| Command                                                     | Description                                                                                                                                                                        |
| ----------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `deploy`                                                    | Validate the definitions, check any generated runtime still matches them, then deploy the selected deployment.                                                                     |
| `deploy --all-partitions`                                   | Deploy every deployment in the config. A failure in one does not stop the rest.                                                                                                    |
| `deploy --check`                                            | Validate local definitions and check the generated runtime, without contacting the dataset.                                                                                        |
| `deploy --dry-run`                                          | Check the generated runtime, then show a diff against what is already deployed, without writing.                                                                                   |
| `deploy --verbose`                                          | Print the full report of the functions the selected deployments need when no generated runtime is here, in place of the summary.                                                   |
| `deploy --only <name>`                                      | Limit deploy, check, or dry-run to one definition. The generated-runtime check still covers the whole config.                                                                      |
| `start <name>`                                              | Start an instance from a deployed definition. Pass `--field` for input values.                                                                                                     |
| `list`                                                      | List instances (in-flight by default). Filter with `--definition`.                                                                                                                 |
| `show <instance-id>`                                        | Show an instance's state, activities, and effects.                                                                                                                                 |
| `diagnose <instance-id>`                                    | Explain why an instance is or isn't progressing, and what would unstick it.                                                                                                        |
| `tail <instance-id>`                                        | Stream new history entries as they land.                                                                                                                                           |
| `abort <instance-id>`                                       | Stop an in-flight instance. Pending effects cancel; the instance stays where it is.                                                                                                |
| `set-stage <instance-id> --to <stage>`                      | Move an instance to a stage, skipping declared transitions. The target stage's enter lifecycle still runs.                                                                         |
| `reset-activity <instance-id> <activity>`                   | Re-run a failed activity, or `--skip` it so a gated transition can fire.                                                                                                           |
| `fire-action <instance-id>`                                 | Fire an action on a waiting activity. Omit `--action` to list what can be fired.                                                                                                   |
| `blueprints generate`                                       | Write the Sanity Blueprints runtime the definitions require next to `sanity.workflow.ts`.                                                                                          |
| `blueprints generate --check`                               | Verify that runtime still matches the definitions. Writes nothing; exits non-zero on any difference.                                                                               |
| `definitions list`                                          | List deployed definitions.                                                                                                                                                         |
| `definitions show <name>`                                   | Show a deployed definition (latest version, or `--version`).                                                                                                                       |
| `definitions validate <file...>`                            | Validate definitions in JSON files without a config, login, or network. `--json` prints the machine-readable report.                                                               |
| `definitions diff <name>`                                   | Diff the in-code definition against what is deployed.                                                                                                                              |
| `definitions delete <name>`                                 | Delete a deployed definition. Refuses while live instances exist unless `--cascade`.                                                                                               |
| `nuke --deployment <name>` / `nuke --partition <partition>` | Dev reset: delete every engine-owned document for that partition (instances, definitions, guards). Prints a plan, then asks for confirmation. Content documents are never touched. |
| `nuke --instance <id>`                                      | Dev reset: delete one finished instance and its guards. Refuses in-flight instances (abort first).                                                                                 |

The `definitions` and `blueprints` commands also answer to the singular
`definition` and `blueprint`, so `definition list` runs `definitions list`.

## Generating the Blueprints runtime

**Experimental, and not ready for production use in this release.** Both
commands are available so you can try the generated runtime and give feedback;
their flags and their output may still change. What you would hit today:

- A start watcher runs for every matching write, and each write starts a new
  instance of every applicable definition, even for a document that already has
  one. Only the definition's own start requirements refuse it, such as a
  `singleSubject` requirement.
- Definitions and functions deploy in two steps, definitions first, until the
  Blueprints service registers the `sanity.workflow` resource.
- A generated file cannot be taken over: editing one is drift, and the next
  generation rewrites it.
- A retry policy is not checked against its function's timeout at generation, so
  an effect can be configured to retry for longer than its function may run.

All of these are tracked, and the next release is the bar for using this in
production.

A definition that declares an effect, reads `$now`, or starts autonomously needs
server-side code: something has to run the effect handlers, sample deadlines, and
start instances from document writes. `blueprints generate` derives that runtime
from the definitions and writes it next to `sanity.workflow.ts`, so
`npx sanity@latest blueprints deploy` has something to deploy. A purely interactive
workflow needs none of it, and the command says so.
Blueprint generation parses `sanity.blueprint.ts` without loading your
project's TypeScript installation. The CLI works beside TypeScript 6 or 7 and
does not require TypeScript for this command.

Five prerequisites:

- **Each deployment is exported under its own `name`, and the export is the
  deployment object itself**, as the [Configuration](#configuration) example
  does: every generated module imports its deployment from `./sanity.workflow`
  by that name. The command refuses to write anything until each name is
  exported, and names the export to add. It checks the name only, so make sure
  each export is the deployment your config lists. A typecheck of the generated
  modules catches a wrong export only where a generated function uses it, and a
  deployment that needs no functions emits none.
- **`sanity.workflow.ts` is importable inside a deployed function.** Every
  generated module imports it, and each function bundles it, so the file runs
  where your shell and your `.env` do not exist. Reading an absent variable
  there yields `undefined`; what fails is a config that **throws** when a
  variable is missing, or requires one to build the deployment, because that
  runs on init before your handler is reached. Keep the deployment's resource
  coordinates literal in the file and read secrets inside your handlers.
- **The Blueprints packages the generated modules import are installed**,
  alongside the CLI and its peers.
- **Your definitions are deployed before the functions.** The generated
  `workflows.blueprint.ts` carries the definitions entry commented out, because
  the Blueprints service does not accept the `sanity.workflow` resource type
  yet, so `npx sanity@latest blueprints deploy` does not deploy them. Run
  `npx @sanity/workflow-cli deploy` first: a function that starts or advances an
  instance resolves its definition from the Content Lake, and finds nothing
  until that deploy has run.
- **A generated heartbeat needs an organization-scoped stack.** The heartbeat is
  a scheduled function, and the platform only accepts one on a stack in
  organization scope. A project-scoped stack refuses it, and with it the whole
  deploy. See
  [Promote a stack to organization scope](https://www.sanity.io/docs/blueprints/promote-stack-to-organization-scope).
  How often it may run is a plan limit rather than something the generator
  chooses — see [the schedule](#the-generated-heartbeats-schedule) below.

```sh
npm install --save-dev @sanity/blueprints @sanity/functions @sanity/workflow-blueprint
npx @sanity/workflow-cli blueprints generate
npx @sanity/workflow-cli deploy
npx sanity@latest blueprints deploy
```

Each generated function's `package.json` copies the specifications your project
declares for `@sanity/functions`, `@sanity/workflow-blueprint`, and
`@sanity/workflow-engine`. A package you declare nowhere fails the command
rather than being stamped with a guessed range.

The command prints what the definitions need, then every file it wrote.

Fill in each `effect-handlers/<effect name>.ts`: they are yours, scaffolded once
and never overwritten. Everything marked `created`, `updated`, or `unchanged`
under `workflows.blueprint.ts`, `functions/`, and `effect-handlers/all.ts` is
regenerated on every run, so edits there do not survive. Your own
`sanity.blueprint.ts` receives the `workflowResources` import and spread once;
after that the command leaves it alone. The command never deletes a file. A
handler for an effect you removed, a scaffold blocked by a path that differs
only in case, and a blueprint it could not wire are reported for you to resolve.
So is a stale function directory: one under `functions/` whose `index.ts`
carries the generator's header but which the definitions no longer produce,
such as the directory a renamed function leaves behind. The generated blueprint
does not deploy it. A directory whose `index.ts` has no generator header is
yours, and is never reported.

The command covers every deployment in the config, because the emitted
`workflows.blueprint.ts` declares them all.

### Where each workflow runs

The report opens with the hosting each `runtime` block resolved to, after every
level has inherited from the one above it. It matters because a name listed
under `durableFunction` or `selfHosted` has no emitted function to point at:

- `function` — a drain, the heartbeat, and the start watchers.
- `durableFunction` — nothing is emitted yet. The rest of the deployment emits
  normally around it.
- `selfHosted` — nothing is emitted, and the report ends with what your own
  process must do instead: which deadlines to tick, which effects to drain,
  which parents to re-evaluate when a child settles, and which autonomous
  definitions to start. The heartbeat ticks only the `'function'`-hosted
  workflows.

### The generated heartbeat's schedule

The heartbeat is emitted on `* * * * *`, one run a minute, and how often the
platform will actually run it is a plan limit rather than something the
generator can choose: Sanity documents the threshold as
[Free daily, Growth hourly, Enterprise minutely](https://www.sanity.io/docs/functions/functions-introduction).
A workflow whose deadlines depend on the heartbeat advances no faster than the
heartbeat runs. An effect no drain picked up becomes eligible to re-queue five
minutes after it was queued, and a later heartbeat run re-queues it; each run
re-queues on at most 30 instances, so a large backlog takes several runs. Check
your plan's cadence before relying on a `$now` deadline in a deployed workflow.

### Checking for drift in CI

`blueprints generate --check` renders the same runtime in memory and compares it
with the files on disk. It writes nothing and exits zero when they match:

```
$ npx @sanity/workflow-cli blueprints generate --check
✔ the generated tree matches the definitions
```

Otherwise it exits `1` and names every file, so the log alone says what to fix:

```
$ npx @sanity/workflow-cli blueprints generate --check
✖ The generated tree does not match the definitions (1):
    differs    effect-handlers/all.ts
  Run `sanity-workflows blueprints generate` to bring it back in line.
$ echo $?
1
```

A file reports `missing` when nothing is at its path, `differs` when the file
there has other contents, and a handler for a declared effect reports `missing`
when you have not written it yet. A stale function directory also fails the
check, and the report names it. Add the command to the job that builds your
blueprint and a definition change can no longer ship without the runtime it
needs.

### Every deploy runs the same check

`deploy` validates the definitions, then looks for `workflows.blueprint.ts` next
to `sanity.workflow.ts`. When that file is there, the deploy runs the same
comparison as [Checking for drift in CI](#checking-for-drift-in-ci), and a
difference stops it:

```
$ npx @sanity/workflow-cli deploy --partition prod
✖ The generated tree does not match the definitions (1):
    differs    workflows.blueprint.ts
  Run `sanity-workflows blueprints generate` to bring it back in line.
$ echo $?
1
```

Nothing is written when that happens: the check runs before the first definition
reaches the dataset, and before the CLI resolves a token. A stale function directory
does not stop the deploy, because the generated blueprint does not deploy it.
The deploy prints a warning naming the directory and continues. Run
`blueprints generate`, review what it wrote, and deploy again.

Definitions deploy first and the functions follow: `sanity-workflows deploy`
writes the definitions, then `npx sanity@latest blueprints deploy` ships the runtime
that serves them. That order is why the deploy is where drift is caught. It is
the step that would otherwise put definitions in front of a runtime that cannot
serve them.

When no `workflows.blueprint.ts` is there, the deploy summarises the functions
the selected deployments need and continues, so a project that has not
generated one yet still deploys:

```
$ npx @sanity/workflow-cli deploy --partition prod
Runtime needs:
  prod (prod) needs 3 Sanity Functions (1 effect drain, 1 heartbeat, 1 start watcher)

⚠ No generated runtime is here. Run `sanity-workflows blueprints generate` to emit one, unless a runtime you maintain yourself already serves these definitions. Pass --verbose for the full report.
```

`deploy --verbose` prints the full report in place of the summary: each
function, what it runs, and why the definitions need it, the same report
`blueprints generate` prints before it writes. Nothing is written either way.
The summary and the report cover the deployments the run selects, so a
deployment needing no functions prints nothing about the runtime even when a
sibling needs some. Definitions no runtime can be derived from at all print a
warning saying so. Either way the deploy continues.

The check has no off switch, by design: the definition deploy is the one moment
every deployment passes through, and a flag would be reached for in exactly the
situation the check exists to catch, which is shipping a definition change whose
runtime was never regenerated. Nothing runs for a hand-written runtime, because
a project that never generated a tree has no `workflows.blueprint.ts` for the
check to compare.

Two consequences worth knowing:

- The check covers the whole config, because the generated tree declares every
  deployment in it. `deploy --deployment one` still holds the tree to every
  deployment's definitions, so a sibling deployment stops it by drifting or by
  failing validation.
- `deploy --check` and `deploy --dry-run` run it too, and the check itself is
  offline in both. `--check` is the complete credential-free pre-flight:
  definitions valid, runtime in line, dataset untouched. `--dry-run` goes on to
  authenticate and read the deployed state to build its diff.

## Telemetry

The CLI collects usage telemetry through Sanity's standard pipeline. Consent
is the account-wide status managed by `npx sanity telemetry enable|disable|status`.
CI and trueish `DO_NOT_TRACK` suppress everything except a deploy that may share
new definitions, which forces that deploy's telemetry unless `--no-share-defs`
is passed — see [Definition sharing](#definition-sharing). A session that isn't
logged in sends nothing. A logged-in run sends whether or not a
`sanity.workflow.ts` is found. A one-time notice on stderr discloses collection
on first use.

What may be collected is governed by [Sanity's telemetry
policy](https://www.sanity.io/telemetry). This package sends a subset of it.

Collected:

- Project id, dataset, and organization id, as session properties. The
  organization id is best effort: it needs a lookup that can resolve to
  nothing, and the event sends either way.
- Operating system, CPU architecture, JavaScript runtime and version, and the
  CLI version.
- The command invoked, and the flags it was given. Each is normalised to its
  canonical long form, so `--partition=prod`, `--partition prod`, and the
  deprecated `--tag prod` all report `--partition=prod`. A flag the command declared, and did not redact, reports its
  **value**; because values ship, a flag naming a definition, stage,
  deployment, document, or user reports that name or id verbatim. Redact a
  flag whose value should not leave the machine.
- Structural counts and closed vocabulary values derived from a definition or
  instance: stage and action counts, activity and field kinds, lifecycle,
  status enums, and durations.
- Content fingerprints of definitions, and random run ids.
- `instanceId`, the instance document `_id`. Engine-minted ids embed the
  deployment partition (`<partition>.wf-instance.<random>`), so the partition
  reaches telemetry through this field. A caller-supplied instance id is sent verbatim.
- The author-chosen effect name, on effect events.

Never collected, because the policy excludes them:

- Environment variables, file paths, and file contents.
- Logs and serialized JavaScript stack traces.

Never collected, because this package goes further than the policy requires.
The policy does not prohibit any of these, so their absence here is this
package's choice and not a company-wide guarantee:

- The value of a redacted flag. A flag whose value is text a person typed
  reports its name alone: `--reason` on `abort`, `set-stage`, and
  `definitions delete`, `--field` on `start`, and `--param` on `fire-action`.
- The value of any flag the command did not declare, including a misspelling
  of a redacted flag. Only the name is reported, and the token after it is
  withheld unless the flag carries its value in the same token (`--resaon=x`,
  `-zx`). The `sanity` CLI sends these whole; withholding them is what keeps
  a mistyped `--reason` from sending the text redaction exists to withhold.
- Anything after the `--` terminator. Those tokens are not reported at all.
- Error messages, and stack traces of any language. The policy permits error
  information that excludes sensitive data, but this package's errors quote
  definition names, partitions, and argv, so none is sent. A failure is reported as
  a success boolean and nothing else.
- Document content, GROQ, and field values.
- Definition names and stage names in the engine's own event payloads. A stage
  transition reports positions in `stages[]`, never names. This does not
  extend to flag values, which ship verbatim as described above.

Note that a dataset name, a deployment partition, and an effect name are all
customer-authored. They are collected deliberately, as identifiers and as a
closed label, not as free text.

Definition sharing sends the definition document to a first-party feedback
endpoint, not through this pipeline; telemetry only records the content-free
markers below.

Each event includes `context.surface: 'cli'`, the `@sanity/workflow-cli`
package version in `context.packageVersion` (also when run as `sanity
workflows`), and its process execution mode in `context.environment`. `NODE_ENV=production` reports `production`;
`development` and `test` report `development`. Unset, empty, and unrecognized
values default to `production` for installed CLI and MCP runs. The SDK reports
build mode and defaults to `development` instead.

When comparing activity across surfaces, group or filter by `context.surface`
alongside `context.environment`. Environment does not identify a production
dataset or deployment; the API host, dataset name, and deployment partition do not
set it. Existing telemetry consent and opt-out settings still apply.

One extension point: supply your own logger as `telemetry` in
`sanity.workflow.ts` and the built-in pipeline is not constructed at all —
every event flows to your implementation unconditionally (CI included), and
consent, suppression, and destination become its business.

### Session properties

The built-in store attaches these user properties once per invocation (joined
to events by session id). User identity is not in the payload; the intake
service resolves the sender from the authenticated session.

| Property          | What it is                                                                                                                                |
| ----------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `surface`         | Always `'cli'`.                                                                                                                           |
| `machinePlatform` | Node `process.platform` (for example `darwin`, `linux`).                                                                                  |
| `cpuArchitecture` | Node `process.arch`.                                                                                                                      |
| `runtime`         | Always `'node'` for this CLI.                                                                                                             |
| `runtimeVersion`  | Node `process.version`.                                                                                                                   |
| `cliVersion`      | The CLI package version, when oclif supplied it.                                                                                          |
| `projectId`       | The `--project-id` the run names, else the first dataset-backed deployment's project in `sanity.workflow.ts`. Absent when neither exists. |
| `dataset`         | The `--dataset` the run names, else that deployment's dataset. Absent when neither exists.                                                |
| `orgId`           | Organization id for that project, when the lookup succeeds before the command flushes. Optional.                                          |

### CLI events

These events are defined by this package.

#### `Workflows CLI Command Executed` (version 2)

One trace per workflows command, shaped like the `sanity` CLI's own
`CLI Command Executed` so both join on the same columns. The built-in store
fixes the invocation's identity as the trace context in the prerun hook and
completes the trace in the finally hook; the context rides every event the
trace emits. Host commands outside the `workflows` topic do not emit.

The context carries:

| Field              | Type       | What is collected                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        |
| ------------------ | ---------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| `groupOrCommand`   | `string`   | Always `'workflows'`.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    |
| `commandArguments` | `string[]` | The oclif command path below the topic: `['deploy']`, `['definitions', 'list']`. Empty for the bare topic and for an invocation oclif resolved to no command. Never argv free-text.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| `extraArguments`   | `string[]` | Each flag on the invocation, in the order given and repeated if repeated, in its canonical `--name=value` form: `--partition prod`, `--partition=prod`, and the deprecated `--tag prod` all report `--partition=prod`. A boolean reports `--name` or `--no-name`. A redacted flag reports `--name` alone, and an undeclared flag reports its name as typed (`--resaon`, `-z`) alone. Tokens after `--` are not reported. |
| `coreOptions`      | `object`   | `{debug, help, version}`. `debug` comes from a set `DEBUG` variable, `help` from a literal `help` token, `version` from `--version`.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |

The payload carries one field, on `trace.log`:

| Field     | Type      | What is collected                                        |
| --------- | --------- | -------------------------------------------------------- |
| `success` | `boolean` | `true` when the command finished without an oclif error. |

A config-supplied logger has no trace, so it receives the four context fields
and `success` together as one log payload.

#### `Workflows CLI Definition Shared` (version 1)

One content-free marker per newly created definition version that actually
reached Sanity's definition-feedback endpoint. Unchanged redeploys, dry runs,
and `--check` never emit it. The document itself is not in this event.

| Field              | Type       | What is collected                                                                                    |
| ------------------ | ---------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `contentHash`      | `string`   | Content fingerprint of the donated definition.                                                       |
| `deployId`         | `string`   | Random run id shared with that invocation's `Workflows Engine Definition Deployed` events.           |
| `stageCount`       | `number`   | Declared stages.                                                                                     |
| `activityCount`    | `number`   | Activities across those stages.                                                                      |
| `actionCount`      | `number`   | Actions across those activities.                                                                     |
| `transitionCount`  | `number`   | Declared transitions.                                                                                |
| `fieldCount`       | `number`   | Declared field entries at workflow, stage, and activity scope.                                       |
| `activityKinds`    | `string[]` | Distinct effective activity kinds, sorted: `user`, `service`, `script`, `manual`, `receive`.         |
| `fieldKinds`       | `string[]` | Distinct declared field kinds, sorted (engine field kinds such as `string`, `subject`, `assignees`). |
| `guardCount`       | `number`   | Guards declared on stages.                                                                           |
| `effectCount`      | `number`   | Effects declared on actions.                                                                         |
| `subworkflowCount` | `number`   | Actions that carry a `spawn` block.                                                                  |
| `lifecycle`        | `string`   | `'standalone'` or `'child'`.                                                                         |

#### `Workflows CLI Definition Sharing Decided` (version 2)

One event per `deploy` that created at least one new definition version,
whether or not anything was donated. Measures opt-out rate without carrying
the document.

| Field             | Type      | What is collected                                                                                                             |
| ----------------- | --------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `decision`        | `string`  | `'opt-in'` (`--share-defs`), `'opt-out'` (`--no-share-defs`), or `'default'` (neither flag).                                  |
| `shared`          | `boolean` | Whether a donation POST reached the endpoint. `false` for any non-sharing decision, and for a chosen share whose POST failed. |
| `definitionCount` | `number`  | Newly created definition versions this invocation could have donated.                                                         |

### Engine events the CLI records

Write commands pass the CLI logger into the engine, so a successful operation
also records the engine's adoption events on the same session. Read commands
(`list`, `show`, `diagnose`, `tail`, `definitions list` / `show` / `diff`) do
not emit engine events. `nuke` deletes engine-owned documents outside those
verbs and does not emit them either.

Every engine event includes:

| Field              | Type     | What is collected                                                                       |
| ------------------ | -------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `executionRuntime` | `string` | The JavaScript runtime the engine detected around itself. Always `'node'` for this CLI. |
| `executionKind`    | `string` | The host the engine was told it is running in. Always `'cli'` for this CLI.             |

Every instance-scoped engine event additionally includes:

| Field                   | Type     | What is collected                                                                                  |
| ----------------------- | -------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `definitionContentHash` | `string` | Content fingerprint of the pinned definition. Omitted when the definition predates fingerprinting. |
| `instanceId`            | `string` | Instance document `_id`.                                                                           |

| Event                                  | Version | When the CLI emits it                                               | Additional payload                                                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| -------------------------------------- | ------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `Workflows Engine Definition Deployed` | 2       | `deploy` for each definition (created or unchanged)                 | Same structural counts as `Workflows CLI Definition Shared`, plus `status`: `'created'` or `'unchanged'`.                                                                                                                               |
| `Workflows Engine Instance Started`    | 2       | `start`, and a `fire-action` that spawns a child                    | `initialFieldCount` (number of caller-supplied initial fields), `viaSpawn` (`true` only for a spawned child), `lifecycle`.                                                                                                              |
| `Workflows Engine Stage Transitioned`  | 2       | A committed hop from `fire-action`, `start` cascade, or `set-stage` | `fromStageIndex`, `toStageIndex` (indexes into `stages[]`, never names), `toIsTerminal`, `isRevisit`, `dwellMs` (milliseconds in the exited stage, omitted if that entry is missing), `via`: `'transition'` or `'setStage'`. Unsampled. |
| `Workflows Engine Action Fired`        | 2       | `fire-action`                                                       | `activityKind` (optional; derived kind of the fired activity), `hasParams` (whether params were supplied — not the params), `cascaded` (auto-transitions in the post-action cascade).                                                   |
| `Workflows Engine Instance Aborted`    | 2       | `abort`                                                             | `changed`: `false` if the instance was already terminal.                                                                                                                                                                                |
| `Workflows Engine Stage Set`           | 2       | `set-stage`                                                         | `changed`: `false` if already at the target stage.                                                                                                                                                                                      |
| `Workflows Engine Activity Reset`      | 2       | `reset-activity`                                                    | `changed`: `false` if already at the target status, or the instance was terminal.                                                                                                                                                       |
| `Workflows Engine Definition Deleted`  | 2       | `definitions delete`                                                | `deletedVersionCount`, `cascadeAbortedCount`, `deletedGuardCount` (guards only when the last version goes).                                                                                                                             |
| `Workflows Engine Effect Completed`    | 2       | `abort` cancelling a pending effect                                 | `effect` (author-chosen name), `status` (`'done'`, `'failed'`, or `'cancelled'`), `origin` (`'action'`), `cascaded`.                                                                                                                    |

The engine also defines `Workflows Engine Field Edited`,
`Workflows Engine Instance Ticked`, `Workflows Engine Effects Drained`, and
`Workflows Engine Effect State Reported`. This CLI does not call those verbs,
so it does not record those events. Field-edit and tick events are sampled at
most once per 60 seconds when some other shell does emit them.

## Definition sharing

Separate from telemetry, a `deploy` that creates new definition versions
donates those documents to Sanity — verbatim (structure, names, titles, GROQ
filters, effect configuration, seeded values), plus their deployment
coordinates (project and dataset, or resource id) — never content documents,
instances, or your auth token. The documents go to Sanity's first-party
definition-feedback endpoint, not the telemetry pipeline; telemetry carries
only a content-free marker (content hash plus structural counts) per shared
definition and a per-invocation decision event.

Sharing is **opt-out in every environment**. Pass `--no-share-defs` to decline
for one invocation. With neither flag, the first interactive deploy prints a
full notice before sending and remembers that the notice was shown; every later
flagless deploy prints a status block showing that sharing is on by default and
showing runnable shell examples for the default, explicit opt-in, and opt-out
forms; the explicit flags suppress the status block. Unattended runs (CI,
`DO_NOT_TRACK`, or a non-TTY pipe) also share by default and print that status
block in their logs.
A flagless deploy or explicit `--share-defs` forces that deploy's telemetry
through the environment gate so donated definitions retain their content-free
markers; account-level `sanity telemetry disable` still applies. A failed share
only warns, never failing a completed deploy.

## Known gaps

- **Not listed in `sanity --help` yet.** Every command runs as
  `sanity workflows <command>`, but the Sanity CLI's help output does not list
  the `workflows` topic. Run `npx @sanity/workflow-cli --help` to see the
  commands.
- **No true bypass.** `set-stage` is the engine's `setStage` admin
  override: it skips the definition's declared transitions and filters, but
  the target stage's enter lifecycle and the post-move cascade still run. A
  true force-set that also bypasses guards + enter effects does not exist
  yet — it needs engine work that hasn't landed.

## Identity

Identity is the token behind the configured client: the engine resolves the
acting user (and their roles) from `/users/me`, so every write is attributed
to whoever the token authenticates — there is no identity injection and no
`--as` impersonation. Alongside that "who", the CLI declares an advisory
"via what": every verb carries
`executionContext: { kind: "cli", id: "workflow-cli" }`, stamped on history
entries as provenance.

## Tech stack

Mirrors the Sanity CLI's stack so the eventual plugin port is small:

- [`@oclif/core`](https://oclif.io) for command definitions, flags,
  help.
- `@oclif/plugin-help` for help output.
- `ora`, `boxen`, `log-symbols`, `console-table-printer` for terminal UX;
  color comes from `node:util`'s `styleText` (no separate color dep).
- `@sanity/cli-core` for timestamp formatting (absolute for detail views, relative
  "… ago" for list tables).
- `diff` for the colored JSON unified diff in `deploy --dry-run`.
